text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 2 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is:
explanation: Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions = 2 mm ÷ 100 = 0.02 mm.

text: Which of the following is NOT a unit of time?
explanation: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, so it is a unit of distance, not time.

text: Arrange the following instruments in the correct ascending order of accuracy:
options: Screw gauge, metre rule, vernier callipers
Vernier callipers, metre rule, screw gauge
Metre rule, vernier callipers, screw gauge
Screw gauge, vernier callipers, metre rule
explanation: The metre rule is least precise, vernier callipers more precise, and the screw gauge is most precise of the three.

text: Which of the following units is NOT a fundamental (base) unit?
explanation: The joule (unit of energy) is a derived unit (kg·m²/s²); kilogram, metre and second are base SI units.

text: Which arrangement correctly orders the metric prefixes milli, centi, kilo and mega by increasing value?
explanation: In increasing order of value: milli (10⁻³) < centi (10⁻²) < kilo (10³) < mega (10⁶).

text: Which combination of main scale division (x) and number of vernier scale divisions (n) gives the smallest (best) least count for a vernier calliper?
explanation: Least count = x/n. Computing each: 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.2 mm — the smallest least count (0.01 mm, the most precise) comes from x = 0.5 mm, n = 50.

text: A student wants to express the height of Mount Everest correctly. Which of the following is the correct way to write it?
explanation: SI unit symbols are written in lower-case without a full stop and without pluralising; 'm' is the correct symbol for metre.

text: The least count of a screw gauge is:
options: Inversely proportional to the pitch of the screw
Directly proportional to the number of divisions on the circular scale
explanation: Least count = pitch ÷ number of circular scale divisions, so it is actually directly proportional to the pitch and inversely proportional to the number of divisions — the opposite of both statements given.

text: How can the least count of a vernier calliper be decreased (made more precise)?
options: By reducing the length of the vernier scale only
By increasing the number of divisions marked on the vernier scale
By using a longer main scale
By decreasing the number of divisions on the vernier scale
explanation: Least count = 1 main scale division ÷ number of vernier scale divisions, so increasing the number of vernier divisions reduces the least count.

text: The pitch of a screw gauge is defined as:
options: The distance moved by the screw along its axis in one complete rotation of the head
The smallest length that can be measured by the instrument
The distance between the screw and the stud
The number of divisions on the circular scale
explanation: Pitch is the linear distance the screw advances for one full rotation of the circular (head) scale.

text: A screw gauge can give a wrong (zero error) reading mainly due to:
options: The head scale having too many divisions
The circular scale not showing a true zero when the jaws/stud are in contact without any object
The screw being made of steel
explanation: If the zero of the circular scale does not coincide with the reference line when the screw faces are just touching, the gauge has a zero error that must be corrected in every reading.

text: Which of these is the biggest measurement of time?
explanation: 1 year (≈365 days) is far greater than 1 mean solar day, 2 microseconds or 1 nanosecond.

text: The distance travelled by a screw along its axis in one complete rotation of its head is called its:
explanation: This distance, by definition, is the pitch of the screw gauge.

text: The least count of a screw gauge is calculated using the formula:
options: Least count = Pitch ÷ Number of divisions on the circular scale
Least count = Number of divisions ÷ Pitch
Least count = Pitch × Number of divisions on the circular scale
Least count = Pitch + Number of divisions
explanation: Least count of a screw gauge equals its pitch divided by the number of divisions on its circular (head) scale.

text: A smaller least count of a measuring instrument means that the instrument:
options: Cannot be used for small objects
explanation: A smaller least count means the instrument can resolve smaller differences in length, i.e. it is more precise.

text: A body starts from rest and covers 150 m in 5 s with uniform acceleration. Its acceleration is:
explanation: Using s = ut + ½at² with u = 0: 150 = ½ × a × 5² = 12.5a, so a = 12 m/s².

text: 1 newton is equal to how many dyne?
explanation: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s² = 1000 g × 100 cm/s² = 100000 g·cm/s² = 10⁵ dyne.

text: A column of mercury 5 mm high exerts what pressure? (Density of Hg = 13.6 × 10³ kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)
The time period (T) and frequency (f) of an oscillating simple pendulum are related by:
explanation: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, which is the reciprocal of the time taken for one oscillation (the time period).

text: The time period of a simple pendulum at a place where acceleration due to gravity is 4 times that on Earth, compared to its time period on Earth, is:
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g), so T is inversely proportional to √g. If g becomes 4 times, T becomes 1/√4 = half.

text: Two simple pendulums of the same effective length have bobs of different masses. If one has time period 0.3 s, the time period of the other (different mass, same length) is:
options: 0.3 s — unchanged, since time period does not depend on mass
explanation: The time period of a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(l/g), depends only on its effective length and g, not on the mass of the bob.

text: A man covers two equal distances of a journey at speeds of 15 km/h and 30 km/h respectively. His average speed for the whole journey is:
explanation: For equal distances, average speed = 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂) = 2×15×30/45 = 20 km/h.

text: The effective length of a seconds pendulum (time period 2 s) on Earth is approximately:
explanation: Using T = 2π√(l/g) with T = 2 s and g = 9.8 m/s² gives l ≈ 0.993 m, approximately 1 metre.

text: The time period of a simple pendulum chiefly depends on its:
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g); the time period depends on the effective length (and g), not on the mass, material or colour of the bob.

text: The time period of a seconds pendulum is 2 s. The time it takes for its bob to move from one extreme position to the other extreme is:
explanation: Moving from one extreme to the other is half an oscillation, which takes T/2 = 2/2 = 1 s.

text: A pendulum bob takes 0.25 s to move from its mean position to one extreme end. What is the time period of the pendulum?
explanation: Moving from mean position to one extreme is a quarter of an oscillation (T/4), so T = 4 × 0.25 = 1 s.

text: The relative density (R.D.) of a body is stated as 3. This means:
options: The density of the body is 3 times the density of water
The body has 3 times the mass of water of the same volume and only that
The volume of the body is 3 cm³
explanation: Relative density = density of substance ÷ density of water, so R.D. = 3 means the body is 3 times as dense as water.

text: A body has a relative density of 3. Its density expressed in SI units is:
explanation: Density = R.D. × density of water = 3 × 1000 kg/m³ = 3000 kg/m³.

text: The density of a substance is 7800 kg/m³. Its density expressed in g/cm³ is:
explanation: To convert kg/m³ to g/cm³, divide by 1000: 7800 ÷ 1000 = 7.8 g/cm³.

text: A substance has a density of 7.8 g/cm³. Its relative density is:
explanation: Relative density equals the density expressed in g/cm³ when compared to water (1 g/cm³), so R.D. = 7.8.

text: A second's pendulum (T = 2 s) makes how many complete oscillations in 25 seconds?
explanation: Number of oscillations = total time ÷ time period = 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5.

text: Pendulum A is on Earth and pendulum B (of equal effective length) is at a place where g is one-fourth that on Earth. The ratio of their time periods, T(A) : T(B), is:
explanation: T ∝ 1/√g, so T(A)/T(B) = √(g(B)/g(A)) = √(1/4) = 1/2, giving the ratio 1:2.

text: The slope of a distance-time graph represents the:
explanation: Speed = distance/time, which is exactly what the slope of a distance-time graph gives.

text: 20 ms⁻¹ is equal to:
explanation: To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6: 20 × 3.6 = 72 km/h.

text: Choose the correct statement about uniform motion:
options: The average and instantaneous velocities do not have the same value in uniform motion
The average and instantaneous velocities have the same value in uniform motion
In uniform motion, the speed is changing at every instant
None of the above is correct
explanation: In uniform motion, velocity is constant, so the average velocity over any interval equals the instantaneous velocity at any instant.

text: If a body returns to its starting point after travelling along a path, its displacement at that moment is:
options: Equal to the total distance travelled
explanation: Displacement is the straight-line distance from the starting point to the final position; if the body is back at its starting point, this is zero, even though the distance travelled is not zero.

text: Velocity is defined as the:
explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with time; it is a vector quantity.

text: The magnitude of velocity equals the magnitude of speed of a body when:
options: The body moves in a circle
The body moves along a straight line without changing direction
explanation: When a body moves in a fixed direction along a straight line, distance equals the magnitude of displacement, so speed equals the magnitude of velocity.

text: A body initially moving with velocity u undergoes uniform acceleration a and reaches velocity v. The displacement S during this time is given by:
explanation: From the third equation of motion v² = u² + 2aS, rearranging gives S = (v² − u²)/2a.

text: Which quantity determines the direction of motion of a body — velocity or acceleration?
explanation: The direction of motion at any instant is given by the direction of the velocity vector, not the acceleration.

text: A car moving with some initial velocity is retarded at a rate of 3 m/s². After 3 s of retardation, its velocity is 6 m/s. The initial velocity was:
A body starts from rest and, with uniform acceleration, travels 32 m in 4 s. Its velocity 15 s after the start is:
explanation: From s = ½at²: 32 = ½ × a × 16, so a = 4 m/s². Then v = u + at = 0 + 4 × 15 = 60 m/s.

text: A truck moves 4 km due east and then 3 km due west. The distance covered and the net displacement are respectively:
explanation: Total distance = 4 + 3 = 7 km. Net displacement = 4 km east − 3 km west = 1 km east.

text: A truck moving at 54 km/h stops in 5 s after brakes are applied (assume constant retardation). Its retardation is:
explanation: 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Retardation = (15 − 0)/5 = 3 m/s².

text: A truck moving at 54 km/h (= 15 m/s) stops in 5 s under constant retardation. The distance covered while braking is:
explanation: Distance = area under v-t graph = ½ × 15 m/s × 5 s = 37.5 m.

text: A jogger moves 500 m in 2 minutes, then 1000 m in the next 30 s along the same straight path, in the same direction. The jogger's average speed for the whole journey is:
explanation: Total distance = 500 + 1000 = 1500 m. Total time = 120 + 30 = 150 s. Average speed = 1500/150 = 10 m/s.

text: Distance is a scalar quantity, while displacement is a:
explanation: Distance has magnitude only (scalar); displacement has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity.

text: Acceleration is a:
explanation: Acceleration has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity.

text: Acceleration due to gravity (g) at a place, for freely falling bodies:
options: Is directly proportional to the mass of the body
Is inversely proportional to the mass of the body
Is independent of the mass of the falling body
explanation: g = GM/R² depends on the mass and radius of the planet, not on the mass of the falling body, so all bodies fall with the same acceleration (ignoring air resistance).

text: A car travels from town A to town B, 200 km apart, in 3 hours, and returns from B to A in 2 hours. Which statement is correct?
options: Average speed is 40 km/h and average velocity is 0
Average speed is 60 km/h and average velocity is 0
Average speed is 50 km/h and average velocity is 0
Average speed is 80 km/h and average velocity is 0
explanation: Average speed = total distance/total time = 400/5 = 80 km/h. Since the car returns to its starting point, net displacement = 0, so average velocity = 0.

text: Anand leaves home at 8:30 a.m. for school, 2 km away, and classes start at 9:00 a.m. If he walks the first kilometre at 3 km/h, at what speed must he walk the second kilometre to reach exactly on time?
explanation: Total time available = 30 min = 0.5 h. First km at 3 km/h takes 1/3 h (20 min), leaving 10 min (1/6 h) for the second km, so required speed = 1 ÷ (1/6) = 6 km/h.

text: An object dropped from a cliff falls with constant acceleration of 10 m/s². Its speed 5 s after being dropped is:
A body is dropped from a height and takes 7 s to reach the ground (g = 10 m/s²). The height from which it was dropped is:
A stone is dropped freely into a river from a bridge and takes 2 s to touch the water (g = 10 m/s²). The height of the bridge above the water is:
explanation: h = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m.

text: A stone is dropped from a bridge 80 m above a river (g = 10 m/s²). The velocity with which it strikes the water is:
A stone is dropped from a bridge 80 m above a river (g = 10 m/s²). The time it takes to reach the water is:
explanation: h = ½gt² ⟹ 80 = ½×10×t² ⟹ t² = 16, so t = 4 s.

text: A car starts from rest and reaches a speed of 50 m/s in 30 s. Its acceleration is:
A car starts from rest, reaches 50 m/s in 30 s, then travels at that speed for a further 20 s. The total distance travelled in 50 s is:
explanation: Distance in acceleration phase = average velocity × time = 25 × 30 = 750 m. Distance at constant speed = 50 × 20 = 1000 m. Total = 750 + 1000 = 1750 m.

text: A bullet hits a sandbox with a velocity of 20 m/s and penetrates 10 cm (0.1 m) before stopping. Its deceleration inside the sandbox is:
explanation: Using v² = u² − 2as with v = 0: 0 = 20² − 2×a×0.1 ⟹ a = 400/0.2 = 2000 m/s².

text: A car in a straight line, starting from a certain displacement-time table, shows displacement 0, 6, 12, 12, 12, 12, 20, 24 m at t = 0 to 7 s. During which time interval is the car's velocity maximum?
explanation: Velocity in each 1 s interval: 6, 6, 0, 0, 0, 8, 4 m/s. The maximum velocity (8 m/s) occurs between 5 s and 6 s.

text: A car moving in a straight line has displacements 0, 6, 12, 12, 12, 12, 20 and 24 m at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 s. How do its average velocities during the first 2 s and the last 2 s compare?
explanation: Average velocity (0–2 s) = (12−0)/2 = 6 m/s. Average velocity (5–7 s) = (24−12)/2 = 6 m/s. They are equal.

text: A sound of frequency 5 Hz is classified as:
explanation: The audible range for humans is roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; 5 Hz is below this, so it is infrasonic.

text: A sound of frequency 500 Hz is classified as:
explanation: 500 Hz lies within the audible range for humans (20 Hz to 20,000 Hz).

text: A force is needed to:
options: Change the velocity of a body
Keep the velocity of a body constant
explanation: By Newton's first law, a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force; a force is needed only to change velocity.

text: Two bodies A and B of the same mass are moving with velocities v and 2v respectively. Compare their inertia and momentum.
options: Inertia is equal; momentum of B is twice that of A
Inertia of B is twice that of A; momentum is equal
Both inertia and momentum of B are twice that of A
explanation: Inertia depends only on mass, which is equal for both, so their inertia is the same. Momentum = mv, so B's momentum (m×2v) is twice A's (m×v).

text: Rimi and Geeta set two balls of masses 3m and m into motion with velocities 2v and v respectively. Compare their inertia and momentum.
options: Inertia and momentum are both equal
explanation: Inertia depends on mass: 3m:m = 3:1. Momentum = mass×velocity: (3m×2v):(m×v) = 6mv:mv = 6:1.

text: When a shot is fired from a gun, the gun recoils backward. This is explained by:
options: The law of conservation of energy only
Newton's third law of motion (equal and opposite reaction)
explanation: The gun exerts a forward force on the bullet (action); by Newton's third law, the bullet exerts an equal and opposite backward force (reaction) on the gun, causing recoil.

text: The inertia of a body depends on its:
explanation: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion, and it depends only on the mass of the body.

text: A ball of mass 100 g rolling at 10 m/s is slowed by friction to 2 m/s in 2 s. The change in momentum of the ball is:
explanation: Change in momentum = m × Δv = 0.1 kg × (10 − 2) m/s = 0.1 × 8 = 0.8 kg·m/s.

text: A ball of mass 100 g rolling at 10 m/s is slowed by friction to 2 m/s in 2 s. The magnitude of the frictional force is:
explanation: Force = change in momentum / time = 0.8 kg·m/s ÷ 2 s = 0.4 N.

text: The two main kinds of inertia are:
options: Inertia of mass and inertia of weight
Inertia of speed and inertia of time
Inertia of rest and inertia of motion
Inertia of force and inertia of energy
explanation: A body at rest tends to stay at rest (inertia of rest) and a moving body tends to keep moving uniformly (inertia of motion); inertia of direction is sometimes listed as a third kind.

text: When you step ashore from a stationary boat, the boat tends to move away from the shore because:
options: Of Newton's third law — you push the boat backward (into the water) as you push yourself forward onto the shore
explanation: As you push against the boat to move forward onto the shore, by Newton's third law the boat experiences an equal and opposite push away from the shore.

text: When a person walks forward on a boat floating in still water, the boat tends to:
options: Move backward (opposite to the direction the person walks)
explanation: By Newton's third law (and conservation of momentum), as the person pushes backward on the boat to move forward, the boat is pushed in the opposite direction.

text: On striking the bottom coin of a pile of carrom coins sharply with a striker, only the bottom coin moves away while the rest of the pile stays almost in place. This is because:
options: The striker only touches the bottom coin and nothing else happens physically
Of the inertia of rest of the upper coins — the short impact time is not enough to set them in motion
The upper coins are glued together
explanation: The force acts for a very short time only on the bottom coin; the inertia of rest of the coins above means they do not have time to move before the bottom coin is gone.

text: Two equal and opposite forces act along the same line on a body moving at a certain velocity. The effect on the body's motion is:
options: No change — it continues moving with the same velocity, since the net force is zero
explanation: Since the two forces are equal and opposite, the net force is zero, so by Newton's first law the body continues with unchanged velocity.

text: People often shake the branches of a tree to make its fruits fall down. This happens because of:
options: The inertia of rest of the fruits, while the shaken branch moves suddenly
explanation: The branch is suddenly set in motion, but the fruits tend to remain at rest (inertia of rest) and so get separated and fall.

text: A cricketer moves his hands backward while catching a fast-moving ball. This is done to:
options: Increase the time of impact, thereby reducing the force on the hands
Increase the force on the ball
explanation: Force = (change in momentum)/time. By increasing the time over which the ball's momentum changes to zero, the cricketer reduces the force experienced.

text: Seatbelts and airbags protect passengers during accidents mainly by:
options: Increasing the time taken for the passenger's momentum to change, thereby reducing the force experienced
Increasing the force on the passenger
explanation: They increase the time over which the passenger decelerates, which (since force = change in momentum/time) reduces the force experienced in a collision.

text: A glass vessel breaks when it falls on a hard floor but does not break when it falls on a carpet from the same height. This is because:
options: The hard floor is heavier than the carpet
The carpet absorbs the vessel's weight
The carpet increases the time of impact, reducing the force on the vessel
Gravity is less near a carpet
explanation: The carpet yields and increases the time taken for the vessel's momentum to become zero, reducing the force (force = change in momentum/time) compared to the sudden stop on a hard floor.

text: When a running car stops suddenly, a passenger tends to be thrown forward. This is because of:
options: The passenger's inertia of motion, which tends to keep them moving forward
The car's acceleration pushing them forward
Friction between the seat and passenger
explanation: The passenger's body tends to continue moving forward (inertia of motion) even as the car stops, until an external force (seatbelt, etc.) acts on them.

text: An athlete running a race continues to run for some distance even after crossing the finishing line. This is due to:
options: A force pushing the athlete forward
explanation: The athlete's body tends to continue in its state of motion (inertia of motion) even after crossing the line, until they consciously slow down.

text: A coin resting on a card placed over a tumbler falls into the tumbler when the card is flicked away quickly. This happens because of:
options: The card pushes the coin down
Air pressure forces the coin down
The coin's inertia of rest — it does not move with the card in the short time the card is flicked away
The coin is attracted by the tumbler
explanation: The card is removed so quickly that the coin (due to inertia of rest) does not move with it, and then falls under gravity into the tumbler.

text: A person falls when they jump out of a moving train. This happens because:
options: Their feet stop suddenly on touching the ground due to friction, while the rest of the body continues moving forward due to inertia of motion
There is no reason; it is random
explanation: On touching the ground, the feet are stopped by friction, but the upper body continues moving forward because of its inertia of motion, causing the person to fall forward.

text: A mass of 2 kg accelerating at 5 m/s² and a mass of 6 kg accelerating at 2 m/s² — which situation needs the greater force?
options: The 6 kg mass at 2 m/s² (12 N)
The 2 kg mass at 5 m/s² (10 N)
Cannot be compared without more data
explanation: F = ma. For the first: F = 2×5 = 10 N. For the second: F = 6×2 = 12 N. The 6 kg mass at 2 m/s² needs the greater force (12 N).

text: An object of mass 100 kg is uniformly accelerated from 5 m/s to 8 m/s in 6 s. The force exerted on the object is:
If the mass of a bus is 2000 kg, the force required to accelerate it at 6 m/s² is:
According to Newton's law of gravitation, the force F between two masses m₁ and m₂ separated by distance r is given by:
explanation: Newton's universal law of gravitation states F = Gm₁m₂/r², where G is the universal gravitational constant.

text: If the distance between two masses triples, the gravitational force between them becomes:
explanation: Since F ∝ 1/r², tripling r reduces F by a factor of 1/3² = 1/9.

text: The gravitational attraction between two bodies at a certain separation is 100 N. If the separation is doubled, the new force is:
explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r reduces F by a factor of 1/2² = 1/4, so new force = 100/4 = 25 N.

text: If the masses of two bodies are doubled and the distance between them is halved, the gravitational force between them becomes:
explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². New F = G(2m₁)(2m₂)/(r/2)² = 4Gm₁m₂ × 4/r² = 16 × original F.

text: Two masses are separated by distance r and attract each other with force F. For the force to become 4F, the new separation should be:
explanation: F ∝ 1/r². For F to become 4F, r² must become r²/4, i.e. r must become r/2.

text: The mass of a body on Earth is 10 kg. On a planet where g = 25 m/s², its mass and weight are respectively:
explanation: Mass is unchanged by location: 10 kg. Weight = mg = 10 × 25 = 250 N.

text: Two balls of masses 3m and 6m move with velocities 4v and 2v respectively. The ratio of their momenta is:
explanation: p₁ = 3m×4v = 12mv; p₂ = 6m×2v = 12mv. The ratio is 1:1.

text: It takes a greater braking force to stop a truck than a motorcycle travelling at the same speed, in the same time. This is because:
options: The truck has a much greater mass, so a larger force is needed to produce the same deceleration (F = ma)
There is no real difference needed
explanation: For the same deceleration a and the same time, F = ma; since the truck's mass is far greater, a much larger force is required.

text: A hydraulic jack has a smaller piston of area 40 cm² carrying a 500 N load, balancing a load on a larger piston. If the larger load is 2500 N, the area of the larger piston is:
explanation: By Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so A₂ = A₁ × F₂/F₁ = 40 × 2500/500 = 200 cm².

text: The larger piston of a hydraulic machine has area 4 m² and carries a load of 400 kgf. If the smaller piston has area 0.01 m², the force required on the smaller piston is:
explanation: By Pascal's law, F_small/A_small = F_large/A_large, so F_small = 400 × 0.01/4 = 1 kgf.

text: In a hydraulic jack, the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the smaller to larger piston (A₁:A₂) is 3:200. To lift a car of weight 400 kgf using this jack, the mass that should be placed on the smaller piston is:
explanation: By Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so F₁ = F₂ × (A₁/A₂) = 400 × (3/200) = 6 kgf.

text: Two containers A and B are filled with the same liquid to heights 1 m and 2 m respectively. Container A's cross-sectional area is twice that of B. The pressures at the bottoms, P₁ (in A) and P₂ (in B), satisfy:
explanation: Liquid pressure at a depth depends only on the height of the liquid column (P = ρgh), not on the cross-sectional area, so the container with the greater height (B, 2 m) has the greater pressure: P₁ < P₂.

text: In a hydraulic machine, the pressures P₁ and P₂ due to the forces F₁ and F₂ on the two pistons of different areas are related as:
explanation: By Pascal's law, the pressure is transmitted equally throughout the liquid, so P₁ = P₂ even though F₁ and F₂ differ (since the piston areas differ).

text: According to Archimedes' principle, the upthrust on a body immersed in a fluid is equal to:
options: The weight of the whole fluid in the container
The weight of fluid displaced by the submerged part of the body
The volume of the submerged part
explanation: Archimedes' principle: the upthrust (buoyant force) on a body equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the submerged part of the body.

text: A body floats partly submerged in liquid A (density ρ₁) and fully submerged (in equilibrium, floating) in liquid B (density ρ₂). The densities ρ₁ and ρ₂ are related as:
explanation: Partly submerged in A means the body's density is less than ρ₁. Fully submerged yet floating in equilibrium in B means the body's density equals ρ₂. So ρ₂ < ρ₁, i.e. ρ₁ > ρ₂.

text: An object is placed, one at a time, in three liquids P, Q and R. In P it is completely submerged and floats in equilibrium; in Q it floats with 1/4 of its volume submerged; in R it floats with 1/2 of its volume submerged. The correct ascending order of the densities of P, Q and R is:
explanation: If the object's density is ρ, then density of P = ρ (fully submerged floating), density of Q = ρ/0.25 = 4ρ, density of R = ρ/0.5 = 2ρ. So ascending order: P (ρ) < R (2ρ) < Q (4ρ).

text: A body of volume V and density ρ is kept completely immersed in a liquid of density ρ_L. If g is the acceleration due to gravity, which expression correctly gives the apparent weight of the body in the liquid?
explanation: Apparent weight = true weight − upthrust = Vρg − Vρ_Lg = V(ρ − ρ_L)g.

text: Which of the following values of atmospheric pressure is INCORRECT?
explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure equals 76 cm Hg (= 760 mm Hg = 760 torr = 1 atm), not 760 cm Hg.

text: A decrease in the barometric (mercury) height in a simple barometer is an indication of:
options: Decrease in the humidity of air
explanation: A fall in atmospheric pressure (shown by falling mercury level) typically indicates the approach of stormy or rainy weather.

text: A gradual increase in the height of mercury in a barometer indicates:
options: The approach of fine, dry weather
explanation: A gradual rise in barometric height indicates rising atmospheric pressure, associated with fine, settled (dry) weather.

text: According to Pascal's law:
options: Pressure at two points at the same depth in a liquid can be different
Pressure at two points at different depths in a liquid is always the same
Pressure cannot change in a confined liquid
Increasing the pressure at any point in a confined liquid increases the pressure at all other points equally
explanation: Pascal's law states that a change in pressure applied at any point of a confined liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished to every other point in the liquid.

text: Pressures at two points A and B in a liquid confined in a cylinder are P₁ and P₂. If the pressure at A is increased by 100 Pa, the pressure at B:
options: Increases by 100 Pa, by Pascal's law
explanation: By Pascal's law, a change in pressure at any point of a confined liquid is transmitted equally to all other points, so B's pressure also increases by 100 Pa.

text: Water shows anomalous expansion in the temperature range:
explanation: Water shows anomalous expansion (density increasing, not decreasing, as it warms) between 0°C and 4°C, with maximum density at 4°C.

text: A block of wood of mass 200 kg floats on water. The density of the wood is 0.8 g/cm³ (800 kg/m³). The total volume of the wooden block is:
explanation: Volume = mass/density = 200/800 = 0.25 m³.

text: A block of wood of mass 200 kg (density 800 kg/m³) floats on water. The volume of the block below the water surface is:
explanation: For a floating body, weight = upthrust, so (mass of body)×g = density of water × V(submerged) × g, giving V(submerged) = mass/density of water = 200/1000 = 0.2 m³.

text: A block of solid floats on water with 3/5 of its volume above the water surface. The density of the solid is:
explanation: Fraction submerged = 1 − 3/5 = 2/5. Density of solid = fraction submerged × density of water = (2/5) × 1000 = 400 kg/m³.

text: A hydraulic press plunger has a cross-sectional area of 12 m² and overcomes a resistive load of 600 kgf. The pump plunger has an area of 2 m². The force needed on the pump plunger is:
explanation: By Pascal's law, F_pump/A_pump = F_load/A_load, so F_pump = 600 × 2/12 = 100 kgf.

text: What should be the ratio of the areas of the smaller cylinder (A₁) to the larger cylinder (A₂) if a force of 50 N on the smaller piston is to overcome a force of 1250 N on the larger piston?
explanation: By Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so A₁/A₂ = F₁/F₂ = 50/1250 = 1/25.

text: A device that works on the principle of transmission of fluid pressure (Pascal's law) is the:
explanation: A hydraulic press or jack uses a confined liquid to transmit and multiply an applied force, based on Pascal's law.

text: The white line painted on the hull of a ship, near the waterline, is known as the:
explanation: The Plimsoll line marks the maximum depth to which a ship may be safely loaded, ensuring it does not become overloaded and unsafe.

text: The hydraulic machine acts as a:
options: Machine with load always equal to effort
explanation: A hydraulic machine uses a small force on a small piston to produce a much larger force on a larger piston, acting as a force multiplier.

text: The SI unit of upthrust is:
explanation: Upthrust is a force, so its SI unit is the newton (N), same as any other force.

text: A body of weight W floats in equilibrium on a liquid. Its apparent weight (weight minus upthrust) is:
explanation: For a body floating freely in equilibrium, the upthrust exactly balances its true weight, so its apparent weight (weight − upthrust) is zero.

text: A solid of density d₁ is placed, in turn, in liquids of densities d₂, d₃ and d₄, where d₁ < d₂ < d₃ < d₄. In which liquid(s) will the apparent weight of the solid be zero?
options: All of them — the solid floats and is in equilibrium in each
explanation: Since the solid is less dense than all three liquids, it floats freely (partly submerged) in equilibrium in each, so its apparent weight is zero in every case.

text: What length of water column exerts the same pressure as 76 cm of mercury? (R.D. of mercury = 13.6)
If the density of ice is 0.9 g/cm³ and the density of sea water is 1.1 g/cm³, the fraction of an iceberg that remains below the surface of the sea water is approximately:
explanation: For a floating body, fraction submerged = density of body/density of liquid = 0.9/1.1 ≈ 0.818, i.e. about 81.8%.

text: An iceberg floats on sea water with 90% of its volume submerged. Compared to the upthrust on it, the weight of the iceberg is:
explanation: For any body floating in equilibrium, its weight exactly equals the upthrust acting on it, regardless of what fraction is submerged.

text: Density and relative density of a substance differ in that:
options: They are always numerically equal in SI units
Density has units (e.g. kg/m³), while relative density is a dimensionless ratio (compared to water)
Relative density has units, density does not
explanation: Density is mass per unit volume with units like kg/m³, while relative density is simply the ratio of a substance's density to that of water, and so has no units.

text: Mercury is preferred over water as the barometric fluid mainly because:
options: Mercury's high density means a much shorter column balances atmospheric pressure (about 76 cm vs over 10 m of water)
Mercury does not evaporate at all
explanation: Since mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, a column of mercury only about 76 cm tall balances atmospheric pressure, compared to over 10 m of water, making the barometer practically sized.

text: A balloon filled with hydrogen rises in air and then stops rising further at a certain height. This happens because:
options: At that height, the density of the surrounding air has decreased enough to equal the effective density of the balloon system, so there is no further net upward force
Hydrogen stops being lighter than air at that height
Gravity becomes zero at that height
The balloon runs out of hydrogen
explanation: Air density decreases with altitude; the balloon stops rising when the upthrust (depending on air density) just balances the total weight of the balloon system.

text: A key difference between the pressure exerted by a solid and that exerted by a fluid (liquid) at rest is that fluid pressure:
options: Is independent of depth, unlike solid pressure
Is always smaller than solid pressure
Acts equally in all directions at a point and increases with depth, unlike solid pressure which acts only in the direction of the applied force
Only acts downward, same as a solid
explanation: A fluid at rest exerts pressure equally in all directions at a given point, and this pressure increases with depth; a solid transmits force only in the direction applied.

text: A hollow iron ball of mass 500 g floats partially submerged in water. The upthrust it experiences is:
explanation: For a body floating in equilibrium, the upthrust equals its weight, so upthrust = 500 gf.

text: A hollow iron ball (average density 0.8 g/cm³) floats in water. The fraction of its total volume that remains submerged is:
explanation: Fraction submerged = density of body/density of water = 0.8/1 = 0.8, i.e. 80%.

text: A hollow iron ball of mass 500 g floats in a liquid whose density is twice that of water. The upthrust it experiences is:
explanation: As long as the ball floats in equilibrium, upthrust equals its weight regardless of the liquid's density, so it remains 500 gf (though less volume is now submerged).

text: A solid iron bar (density about 7.8 g/cm³) floats in mercury (density 13.6 g/cm³) even though it sinks in water. This is because:
options: The density of iron is less than that of mercury but greater than that of water
explanation: A body floats in a liquid only if its density is less than that of the liquid; iron's density (~7.8) is less than mercury's (13.6) but greater than water's (1), so it floats in mercury but sinks in water.

text: A bowl made from the same steel that sinks as a solid piece can float in water when shaped into a bowl. This is because:
options: The bowl shape increases the volume of water displaced for the same mass, reducing the effective density below that of water
explanation: Shaping the steel into a hollow bowl greatly increases the volume it occupies (and hence the volume of water it can displace) without changing its mass, so its effective (average) density becomes less than water's, allowing it to float.

text: The apparent weight (weight in a given fluid) of a body that sinks in both water and kerosene is less in water than in kerosene. This is because:
options: The body weighs less in air near water
There is no real reason; it is random
Water is denser than kerosene, so it provides a greater upthrust, reducing the apparent weight more
explanation: Since water (1 g/cm³) is denser than kerosene (~0.8 g/cm³), it displaces liquid of greater weight for the same submerged volume, giving a larger upthrust and hence a smaller apparent weight in water.

text: Upthrust on a body increases with an increase in the portion of the body submerged in the fluid because:
options: Upthrust is independent of submerged volume
Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced, which increases as the submerged volume increases
Upthrust depends only on the shape of the body
explanation: Upthrust = density of fluid × submerged volume × g, so it increases directly with the volume of fluid displaced, i.e. the submerged volume.

text: A man first swims in sea water, then in river water. Compared to river water, in sea water he would find it:
options: Easier to swim, since denser sea water provides greater upthrust for the same submerged volume
Equally easy, as upthrust is unaffected by density
Harder to swim, since sea water is denser
explanation: For the same submerged volume, denser sea water displaces more weight of liquid, giving a greater upthrust and making it easier to stay afloat and swim.

text: A man swims first in sea water, then in river water, each time floating with part of his body submerged. Comparing the weight of water he displaces in the two cases, in equilibrium:
options: The weight of water displaced is the same in both cases, equal to his own body weight
He displaces more weight of water in sea water
He displaces more weight of water in river water
Weight of water displaced cannot be compared
explanation: Whenever a body floats in equilibrium, the weight of liquid displaced (the upthrust) exactly equals its own weight, regardless of which liquid it floats in.

text: The upthrust experienced by a body immersed in a liquid is directly proportional to:
options: Only the total volume of the body, submerged or not
The volume of the body actually submerged and the density of the liquid
The weight of the body in air, regardless of the liquid
Only the shape of the body
explanation: Upthrust = density of liquid × submerged volume × g, so it depends directly on the submerged volume and the liquid's density.

text: Is the value of 1 kgf the same on Earth and on the Moon?
options: No, because g on the Moon is different, so 1 kgf is smaller there
Yes, because mass does not change
No, kgf has no meaning on the Moon
Yes, because 1 kgf is defined using a fixed standard value of g (9.8 m/s²), independent of location
explanation: By convention, 1 kgf is defined as the force equal to mass (1 kg) times the standard value of g (9.8 m/s²), a fixed reference value, so it is the same everywhere, including on the Moon.

text: A metal piece weighs 200 gf in air and 150 gf when completely immersed in water. Its relative density is:
explanation: R.D. = weight in air / loss of weight in water = 200/(200−150) = 200/50 = 4.

text: A metal piece weighs 200 gf in air and 150 gf in water (R.D. = 4). Its weight when fully immersed in a liquid of density 0.8 g/cm³ would be:
explanation: Volume = loss of weight in water/density of water = 50 cm³. Weight of this volume of the 0.8 g/cm³ liquid displaced = 50 × 0.8 = 40 gf. Apparent weight = 200 − 40 = 160 gf.

text: A solid weighs 144 gf in air and 100 gf when completely immersed in water. The upthrust on it is:
explanation: Upthrust = loss of weight in water = 144 − 100 = 44 gf.

text: A solid weighs 144 gf in air and 100 gf in water. Its volume is:
explanation: Since density of water is 1 g/cm³, volume = upthrust (in gf) ÷ density of water = 44/1 = 44 cm³.

text: A solid weighs 144 gf in air and 100 gf in water. Its relative density is approximately:
explanation: R.D. = weight in air/loss of weight in water = 144/44 ≈ 3.27, approximately 3.3.

text: Two metallic blocks A and B of mass 20 g each are placed in water. Block A is hollow with volume 24 cm³. Does block A float or sink in water?
options: Floats, because it is hollow regardless of density
Sinks, since metal is always denser than water
Floats, since its density (20/24 ≈ 0.83 g/cm³) is less than water's
explanation: Density of A = mass/volume = 20/24 ≈ 0.83 g/cm³, which is less than water's density (1 g/cm³), so block A floats.

text: Block B (mass 20 g, density 5 g/cm³) is placed fully submerged in water. The upthrust on block B is:
explanation: Volume of B = mass/density = 20/5 = 4 cm³. Upthrust = density of water × volume = 1 × 4 = 4 gf.

text: Block B (mass 20 g, upthrust 4 gf when fully submerged in water) has an apparent weight in water of:
explanation: Apparent weight = true weight − upthrust = 20 − 4 = 16 gf.

text: A piece of iron of density 7.8 g/cm³ and volume 100 cm³ is weighed in air. Its weight is:
explanation: Weight (in gf) numerically equals mass in g = density × volume = 7.8 × 100 = 780 g, i.e. 780 gf.

text: A piece of iron of density 7.8 g/cm³ and volume 100 cm³ is completely immersed in water. The upthrust on it is:
explanation: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = density of water × volume = 1 × 100 = 100 gf.

text: A piece of iron of density 7.8 g/cm³, volume 100 cm³, weighs 780 gf in air and experiences an upthrust of 100 gf in water. Its apparent weight in water is:
explanation: Apparent weight = weight in air − upthrust = 780 − 100 = 680 gf.

text: An aluminium can (density 2.7 g/cm³) floats in mercury (density 13.6 g/cm³). The fraction of its volume that remains immersed in mercury is approximately:
explanation: Fraction immersed = density of aluminium/density of mercury = 2.7/13.6 ≈ 0.199, approximately 0.2 (1/5).

text: Water pipes in colder countries often burst in winter. This is because:
options: Cold water flows faster, increasing pressure
Pipes contract more than the water inside
Water expands on freezing into ice (anomalous expansion), and the increased volume cracks the pipe
explanation: Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes into ice; this increase in volume inside a closed pipe can crack it.

text: An egg sinks in fresh water but floats in a strong salt solution. This is because:
options: Salt water is lighter than fresh water
The density of the egg lies between the density of fresh water and that of the strong salt solution
The egg becomes lighter in salt water
explanation: The egg's density is greater than fresh water's (so it sinks) but less than the denser salt solution's (so it floats there).

text: The type of radiation mainly absorbed by greenhouse gases (contributing to the greenhouse effect) is:
options: Infrared radiation emitted by the Earth
explanation: Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming sunlight but absorb the infrared radiation re-emitted by the Earth's surface, trapping heat.

text: Which of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?
explanation: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas; CO₂, methane and water vapour all trap infrared radiation and contribute to the greenhouse effect.

text: Deep pond water has its top layer frozen in winter. The temperature of the water layer just in contact with the ice, and at the bottom of the pond, are respectively:
explanation: The layer touching the ice is at 0°C, while water at 4°C (its maximum density) sinks to the bottom, keeping the bottom at about 4°C — this is why aquatic life can survive under frozen ponds.

text: First law of thermodynamics states that:
options: Entropy of an isolated system always increases
Heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by it (energy is conserved)
Heat always flows from a cold to a hot body
Energy can be created but not destroyed
explanation: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of conservation of energy: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW.

text: The second law of thermodynamics implies that heat flows spontaneously, without external work, from a:
options: Hotter body to a colder body
Hotter body to an even hotter body
Colder body to a hotter body
explanation: The second law of thermodynamics states that heat flows spontaneously only from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature, never the reverse without external work.

text: The SI unit of heat is the joule (J). It is related to the older unit, the calorie, as:
explanation: 1 calorie is defined as approximately 4.186 joules, the mechanical equivalent of heat.

text: The most non-polluting and energy-efficient lighting device among the following is:
explanation: LED lamps convert the largest fraction of electrical energy into light with the least waste heat and no toxic mercury content, making them the most efficient and least polluting choice.

text: As a bulb's filament glows (heats up), its resistance:
explanation: The resistance of a metallic filament increases as its temperature rises, which is why a hot, glowing filament has higher resistance than when cold.

text: Temperature of a body determines:
options: Only the average kinetic energy of its particles
Its thermal state, the average kinetic energy of its particles, and the direction of heat flow
Only the direction of heat flow
explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of a body's particles, defines its thermal state, and determines the direction in which heat will flow when in contact with another body.

text: Among 0°C, 4°C, 10°C and room temperature, water (of a fixed mass) has its maximum volume at:
explanation: Water has minimum volume (maximum density) at 4°C. Below 4°C (down to 0°C) it expands anomalously, and above 4°C it expands normally with rising temperature, so among these options its volume is greatest at room temperature.

text: A uniform cube of side 2 cm is immersed in water with its top surface at a depth of 5 cm. Taking density of water = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s², the pressure at the top surface of the cube is:

A cube of side 2 cm is immersed in water with its top face 5 cm below the surface (density of water 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²). The resultant thrust on the cube due to the pressure difference between its bottom and top faces is:
explanation: Pressure at bottom (depth 7 cm) = 1000×10×0.07 = 700 Pa. Resultant pressure = 700 − 500 = 200 Pa. Resultant thrust = pressure × area of face = 200 × (0.02×0.02) = 200 × 0.0004 = 0.08 N.

text: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
explanation: A plane mirror always forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object, which is laterally inverted (left-right reversed).

text: The pole of a spherical mirror is:
options: The line joining focus and centre of curvature
The centre of the sphere from which the mirror is cut
A point on the radius of curvature only
The midpoint on the principal axis where the mirror surface meets it
explanation: The pole is the geometric centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface, lying on the principal axis.

text: A man stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror. The distance between the man and his image is:
explanation: The image forms 3 m behind the mirror, as far behind as the object is in front, so the total separation between the man and his image is 3 + 3 = 6 m.

text: An object is placed 80 cm in front of a plane mirror. The mirror is then moved 45 cm further away from the object. By how much does the image shift (in its position, not relative to the object)?
explanation: Image position = 2 × (mirror distance from object). Initially 2×80 = 160 cm from the object; after the mirror moves to 125 cm away, image position = 2×125 = 250 cm. Shift = 250 − 160 = 90 cm.

text: In the dial of a clock, with lines marked instead of numbers, a plane mirror shows the reflected time as 4:25. The actual time is:
explanation: For a clock reflected in a mirror, actual time = 11:60 − reflected time = 11:60 − 4:25 = 7:35.

text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at an angle of 30° to each other. The number of images formed of an object placed between them is:
explanation: Since 360°/30° = 12 (an even integer), the number of images = 12 − 1 = 11 (the same for symmetric or asymmetric placement).

text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 50° to each other, with an object placed between them. The number of images formed (same whether placed symmetrically or asymmetrically, since 360°/50° is not a whole number) is:
explanation: 360°/50° = 7.2, which is not an integer; in this case the number of images formed equals the integer (floor) part of this value, i.e. 7, the same for both symmetric and asymmetric placement.

text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 72° to each other, with an object placed asymmetrically between them. The number of images formed is:
explanation: 360°/72° = 5, an odd integer. For asymmetric placement with an odd integer ratio, the number of images = 5.

text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 45° to each other. The number of images formed, whether the object is placed symmetrically or asymmetrically, is:
explanation: 360°/45° = 8, an even integer, so the number of images = 8 − 1 = 7, the same for symmetric and asymmetric placement.

text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 60° to each other, with an object placed between them. The number of images formed, same for symmetric and asymmetric placement, is:
explanation: 360°/60° = 6, an even integer, so the number of images = 6 − 1 = 5, the same for symmetric and asymmetric placement.

text: A virtual and enlarged image can be obtained using a:
explanation: A concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is placed between the pole and the focus.

text: When a concave mirror is used as a shaving mirror, the person's face (relative to the mirror's focus) should be located:
options: Between the pole and the focus
Between the centre of curvature and focus
explanation: Placing the face between the pole and focus of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect and magnified image, ideal for shaving.

text: When an object is placed between the pole and focus of a concave mirror, the image formed is:
options: Real, erect and the same size
explanation: For an object between the pole and focus of a concave mirror, the image is always virtual, erect and magnified, formed behind the mirror.

text: Assertion (A): When a concave mirror is used as a shaving mirror, the face should lie between the pole and focus. Reason (R): An object placed within the focal length of a concave mirror forms a real and enlarged image.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: A is correct (face between pole and focus for shaving). However, R is false: an object between pole and focus of a concave mirror forms a virtual (not real) enlarged image.

text: Assertion (A): Focal length of a convex mirror is taken as positive. Reason (R): The focus of a convex mirror lies behind the mirror.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
explanation: By the New Cartesian sign convention, distances measured behind the mirror (where the convex mirror's focus lies) are positive, so A is true and R is the correct reason.

text: The image formed by a convex mirror of an object placed at a finite distance in front of it is always:
explanation: A convex mirror always diverges reflected rays, so it forms a virtual, erect, diminished image regardless of the object's position.

text: One common practical use of a convex mirror is as a:
options: Vehicle rear-view/side mirror, for its wide field of view
explanation: Because a convex mirror always forms a diminished, erect image showing a wider field of view, it is commonly used as a rear-view or side mirror in vehicles.

text: Which type of mirror does a dentist typically use to examine a patient's teeth?
options: Convex mirror, for a wide field of view
Plane mirror, for a same-size image
Concave mirror, to get a magnified image of the teeth
explanation: A concave mirror, with the teeth placed between its pole and focus, gives a magnified virtual image, helping the dentist see small details clearly.

text: Which type of mirror is commonly used as a reflector for street lights, to spread light over a wide area of the street?
explanation: A convex reflector diverges light over a wide area, which is useful for spreading illumination across a street.

text: A converging (concave) mirror forms a real image of height 4 cm of a 1 cm tall object placed 20 cm from the mirror. The image distance is:
explanation: Magnification m = image height/object height = 4/1 = 4. Since m = v/u for a real image, v = 4 × 20 = 80 cm.

text: A concave mirror forms a real image of height 4 cm (4 times a 1 cm object) placed 20 cm away, with the image at 80 cm. The focal length of the mirror is:
An object of height 4 cm is placed 40 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 24 cm. The position of the image is:
An object 4 cm tall is placed 40 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 24 cm, and the image forms at 60 cm. The size of the image is:
explanation: Magnification m = v/u = 60/40 = 1.5. Image height = 1.5 × 4 cm = 6 cm.

text: An object is placed 40 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 24 cm, and the image forms 60 cm from the mirror (beyond C at 48 cm). The nature of the image is:
explanation: Since the image distance (60 cm) is real (positive, in front of the mirror) and larger than the object, the image is real, inverted and magnified.

text: If the image is formed 6 cm from a concave mirror, with the object at 12 cm in front of it, the focal length of the mirror is:
An object is 12 cm in front of a concave mirror and its image forms 6 cm from the mirror (f = 4 cm). The magnification is:
explanation: Magnification m = v/u = 6/12 = 0.5.

text: An object is 12 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 4 cm, and the image forms at 6 cm (m = 0.5). The nature of the image is:
explanation: Since the image distance is real (positive) and the magnification is less than 1, the image is real, inverted and diminished (object was placed beyond the centre of curvature).

text: A concave mirror produces a 3-times magnified real image of an object placed 10 cm in front of it. The image is located at:
explanation: For a real image, magnification m = v/u, so v = 3 × 10 = 30 cm in front of the mirror.

text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature 12 cm. Using the New Cartesian sign convention (f = +6 cm), the image is formed at:
explanation: f = R/2 = 6 cm (positive, behind, convex). Using 1/v = 1/f − 1/u with u = −30: 1/v = 1/6 − 1/(−30) = 1/6 + 1/30 = 6/30 = 1/5, so v = 5 cm (behind the mirror).

text: An object is 30 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 6 cm, and the virtual image forms 5 cm behind the mirror. The magnification is:
explanation: m = −v/u = −(+5)/(−30) = +1/6. The positive sign shows the image is erect (virtual) and the value shows it is one-sixth the size of the object.

text: A convex mirror's side mirror on a car has radius of curvature 10 m. Another car, 15 m away and 2 m tall, is seen in it. The distance of the image from the mirror is:
A car 2 m tall is 15 m from a convex side mirror of focal length 5 m, and its image forms 3.75 m behind the mirror. The height of the image is:
explanation: Magnification m = v/u (magnitude) = 3.75/15 = 0.25. Image height = 0.25 × 2 m = 0.5 m.

text: The negative sign in the value of the magnification of a mirror indicates that the image is:
explanation: By convention, a negative magnification indicates a real, inverted image, while a positive magnification indicates a virtual, erect image.

text: According to the laws of reflection of light:
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both rays lie in the same plane as the normal
The angle of incidence is always greater than the angle of reflection
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal need not lie in the same plane
explanation: The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.

text: A ray of light is incident at 35° to a plane reflecting surface (measured from the surface). The angle of incidence (measured from the normal) and angle of reflection are:
explanation: The angle from the normal = 90° − 35° = 55°. By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so both are 55°.

text: The focus of a concave mirror is defined as:
options: The midpoint of the mirror's surface
The point on the principal axis where parallel rays (parallel to the principal axis) converge after reflection
The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part
A point outside the principal axis
explanation: The focus (principal focus) is the point on the principal axis where incident rays parallel to the axis converge (concave mirror) or appear to diverge from (convex mirror) after reflection.

text: The centre of curvature of a spherical mirror is:
options: The same as the pole of the mirror
The midpoint between the pole and the focus
The centre of the sphere of which the mirror's reflecting surface is a part
explanation: The centre of curvature is the centre of the hollow glass sphere from which the spherical mirror is cut.

text: If u, v and R denote the object distance, image distance and radius of curvature of a spherical mirror, the correct mirror relation between them is:
explanation: From the mirror formula 1/u + 1/v = 2/R, rearranging gives (u+v)/(uv) = 2/R, i.e. R = 2uv/(u+v).

text: If the image of an object on the principal axis of a concave mirror is formed at the same point as the object, but inverted, the object must be located at:
explanation: Only when an object is placed at the centre of curvature does a concave mirror form a real, inverted image of the same size at the same point.

text: When an object on the principal axis of a concave mirror forms an inverted image at the same point as itself, the distance between the object and the pole is called the:
explanation: The distance from the pole to the centre of curvature is, by definition, the radius of curvature of the mirror.

text: If a concave mirror and the real object it is imaging are both immersed together in water, the position of the real image formed:
options: Remains unchanged, since the laws of reflection do not depend on the surrounding medium
explanation: Unlike refraction through a lens, reflection from a mirror obeys the same laws regardless of the medium, so the image position is unaffected by immersing the mirror and object in water.

text: As you move your face slowly away from the inner (concave) surface of a shiny spoon, the image of your face changes from:
options: Large, erect and virtual (close up) to small, inverted and real (farther away)
explanation: Close to the spoon's concave surface (within its focal length) the image is virtual, erect and magnified; moving beyond the focus produces a real, inverted, diminished image.

text: Both a plane mirror and a convex mirror can form virtual images. The virtual image formed by a convex mirror differs from that of a plane mirror because it is:
options: Diminished (smaller than the object), unlike the plane mirror's same-size image
explanation: A plane mirror's virtual image is always the same size as the object, whereas a convex mirror's virtual image is always diminished.

text: The speed of sound in a gas is independent of the:
explanation: At constant temperature, a change in pressure changes the density in the same proportion, so the speed of sound (v = √(γP/ρ)) is unaffected by pressure.

text: The speed of sound in steel is 5000 m/s. The distance it covers in steel in 9 s is:
explanation: Distance = speed × time = 5000 × 9 = 45000 m = 4.5 × 10⁴ m.

text: The speed of sound in a gas:
options: Increases with an increase in pressure
Decreases with an increase in temperature
Remains unchanged with a change in pressure
Increases with a decrease in humidity
explanation: Speed of sound in a gas does not depend on pressure (at constant temperature); it increases with temperature and with humidity.

text: Choose the correct statement:
options: Sound and light both do not require a medium for propagation
Speed of sound in air is greater than speed of light in air
Light waves are longitudinal mechanical waves whereas sound waves are transverse electromagnetic waves
Speed of light decreases in an optically denser medium, while speed of sound is greatest in solids, less in liquids and least in gases
explanation: Light slows down in optically denser media; sound, a mechanical wave, travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. The other statements are all false.

text: Which of the following statements about sound waves is INCORRECT?
options: They require a material medium for propagation
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot travel through a vacuum at all, so 'they travel fastest in vacuum' is incorrect.

text: Supersonic objects:
options: Produce sound of frequency less than 20 Hz
Travel with speeds greater than the speed of sound in air (about 330 m/s)
Produce sound of frequency between 20 Hz and 20 kHz
Produce sound of frequency greater than 20 kHz
explanation: 'Supersonic' refers to speed — an object moving faster than sound in air. Frequencies above 20 kHz are 'ultrasonic', below 20 Hz 'infrasonic'.

text: Which has the higher frequency — ultrasonic sound or infrasonic sound?
explanation: Ultrasonic sound has frequency above 20 kHz, while infrasonic sound has frequency below 20 Hz.

text: Humans cannot hear the sound produced by the vibrations of a seconds pendulum because:
options: Its frequency (0.5 Hz) is below the lower limit of human hearing (20 Hz)
explanation: A seconds pendulum has T = 2 s, so f = 1/T = 0.5 Hz, which is far below the audible range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

text: A wave pulse of frequency 200 Hz on a string moves a distance of 8 m in 0.05 s. The velocity of the pulse is:
explanation: Velocity = distance/time = 8/0.05 = 160 m/s.

text: A wave of frequency 200 Hz travels on a string at 160 m/s. Its wavelength is:
A wave pulse of frequency 100 Hz on a string moves 5 m in 0.05 s. The velocity of the pulse and the wavelength of the wave are respectively:
The time period of a wave is 0.002 s. Its frequency is:
The correct relationship between wave velocity (v), frequency (f) and wavelength (λ) is:
explanation: A wave travels one wavelength in one time period, so v = λ/T = fλ.

text: If the distance between two consecutive crests of a wave is 5 mm, its wavelength is:
explanation: Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive crests (or troughs), so λ = 5 mm.

text: Spectators at a cricket match hear the sound of the bat hitting the ball a little after they see the stroke. This is because:
options: Light travels much faster than sound in air
Sound is reflected by the ground first
The eyes react faster than the ears
explanation: Light (3 × 10⁸ m/s) reaches the spectators almost instantly, while sound (about 340 m/s) takes noticeably longer to cover the same distance.

text: The SI unit of frequency is:
explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz; 1 Hz is one complete oscillation (vibration) per second.

text: The amplitude of a wave is:
options: The maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its mean position
The distance between two consecutive crests
The number of vibrations per second
The time taken for one vibration
explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the vibrating particles on either side of their mean (rest) position.

text: The audible range of frequency for normal human ears is:
explanation: Normal human ears can hear sounds of frequency roughly between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.

text: How long does sound take to travel along a 1 km iron rail if the speed of sound in iron is 5000 m/s?
explanation: t = distance/speed = 1000/5000 = 0.2 s.

text: A wave pulse has velocity 80 m/s and wavelength 0.2 m. Its frequency is:
A wave pulse travelling at 80 m/s covers what distance in 5 s?
explanation: Distance = speed × time = 80 × 5 = 400 m.

text: The speed of sound in air is 320 m/s and in water is 1600 m/s. The ratio of the distances travelled by sound in air and in water in the same time is:
explanation: In equal time, distance ∝ speed, so the ratio is 320:1600 = 1:5.

text: Speed of sound depends upon the:
options: Temperature of the source producing the sound
Temperature and pressure of the medium
explanation: Speed of sound in a medium depends on the medium's temperature (it is independent of pressure at constant temperature and of the source's temperature).

text: A wave in a slinky of length 5 m travels to one end and back (to and fro) in 5 s. The speed of the wave is:
explanation: To and fro covers 2 × 5 = 10 m in 5 s, so speed = 10/5 = 2 m/s.

text: SONAR uses which type of sound waves?
explanation: SONAR uses ultrasonic waves (above 20 kHz), which have short wavelengths, travel in narrow beams and reflect well from underwater objects.

text: In a longitudinal wave, compressions are regions of:
explanation: In a compression the particles of the medium are crowded together, so both density and pressure are higher than normal.

text: Which of the following statements about the speed of sound is correct?
options: Speed of sound increases with an increase in the density of the gas
Speed of sound increases with an increase in the amplitude of the wave
Speed of sound in air decreases with increase in humidity
Speed of sound increases with an increase in the temperature of the gas
explanation: Speed of sound in a gas increases with temperature. It increases (not decreases) with humidity, decreases with greater density, and is independent of amplitude.

text: An increase in the humidity of air causes the speed of sound in air to:
explanation: Moist air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, so sound travels faster in humid air.

text: A source produces 50 crests and 50 troughs in 0.5 s. The frequency of the wave is:
explanation: One crest plus one trough make one complete wave, so 50 waves are produced in 0.5 s: f = 50/0.5 = 100 Hz.

text: A wave of frequency 100 Hz travels at 150 m/s. Its wavelength is:
One application of ultrasound is:
explanation: Ultrasound is used in SONAR to find sea depth/objects and in medical ultrasonography, among other uses such as cleaning delicate parts.

text: Two requisites of a medium for the propagation of sound are that it must possess:
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave; the medium must be elastic (to restore displaced particles) and have inertia/density (so particles overshoot and keep the vibration going).

text: A radar signal is received 2 × 10⁻⁵ s after it was sent and reflected by an aeroplane. If the waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, how far away is the aeroplane?
explanation: The signal goes to the plane and back, so distance = (v × t)/2 = (3 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁵)/2 = 3000 m.

text: A SONAR pulse is detected 2 s after emission, after reflection from the sea bed. If the speed of sound in water is 1530 m/s, the depth of the water is:
explanation: Depth = (v × t)/2 = (1530 × 2)/2 = 1530 m, because the pulse travels down and back up.

text: A child strikes one end of an aluminium rod and another child at the other end hears two sounds. If sound travels at 346 m/s in air and 6420 m/s in aluminium, the ratio of the time taken through air to that through aluminium is about:
explanation: For the same distance, time ∝ 1/speed, so t(air)/t(Al) = 6420/346 ≈ 18.6. Sound through air takes about 18.6 times as long.

text: If the density of oxygen is 16 times that of hydrogen (same temperature and pressure), the speed of sound in hydrogen compared to that in oxygen is:
The difference between 'ultrasonic' and 'supersonic' is that:
options: Ultrasonic refers to sound of frequency above 20 kHz, while supersonic refers to a speed greater than the speed of sound
Both mean a frequency above 20 kHz
Supersonic refers to frequency below 20 Hz
Ultrasonic refers to a speed greater than the speed of sound
explanation: 'Ultrasonic' describes frequency (above the audible range); 'supersonic' describes the speed of an object moving faster than sound.

text: Sound travels in air at 340 m/s. The wavelength in air of sound from a 20 kHz source is:
A 20 kHz sound source is placed in a water tank, where sound travels at 1500 m/s. The wavelength of the sound in water is:
explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change, so λ = 1500/20000 = 0.075 m = 7.5 cm.

text: The speed of sound in water is 1360 m/s. The time taken by sound to travel 1700 m in water is:
explanation: t = distance/speed = 1700/1360 = 1.25 s.

text: If sound travels 1700 m in air in 5 s, the speed of sound in air is:
explanation: Speed = distance/time = 1700/5 = 340 m/s.

text: A wave of time period 5 s travels with velocity 20 m/s. Its frequency is:
For a wave of time period 5 s travelling at 20 m/s, the distance between a crest and the adjoining trough is:
explanation: λ = vT = 20 × 5 = 100 m. A crest and its adjoining trough are half a wavelength apart: 100/2 = 50 m.

text: In the same medium, how do ultrasonic and infrasonic waves compare in wavelength?
options: Ultrasonic waves have shorter wavelengths, infrasonic waves have longer wavelengths
explanation: In a given medium the speed is the same, so λ = v/f: higher-frequency ultrasonic waves have shorter wavelengths than low-frequency infrasonic waves.

text: Sound travels faster on a:
explanation: Speed of sound in air increases with temperature, so it is greater on a hot day.

text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a primary cell?
options: Chemical energy is converted into electrical energy
Its internal resistance is very low
explanation: Primary cells have a relatively high internal resistance; the other three statements are true of primary cells.

text: A rheostat is used to:
options: Measure the potential difference across the terminals
Measure the magnitude of current in the circuit
Control (vary) the amount of current flowing in the circuit
explanation: A rheostat is a variable resistance; changing its resistance changes, and so controls, the current in the circuit.

text: The magnetic field of an electromagnet can be increased by:
options: Increasing the number of turns in the coil
Reversing the direction of current in the coil
Decreasing the current in the coil
Using alternating current of high frequency
explanation: The strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns of the coil (and with the current); reversing the current only reverses its polarity.

text: Which of the following statements is NOT true?
options: At a neutral point, the resultant magnetic field is zero
An electromagnet is made of soft iron
explanation: Like poles repel each other; only unlike poles attract. The other statements are true.

text: The device used to measure the potential difference between two points of a circuit is the:
explanation: A voltmeter, connected in parallel across two points, measures the potential difference between them.

text: According to Ohm's law, at a given temperature:
options: Potential difference is inversely proportional to the resistance of a conductor
Potential difference is directly proportional to the current flowing through a conductor
Current is directly proportional to the resistance of the conductor
explanation: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, V ∝ I, i.e. V = IR with R constant.

text: At neutral points:
options: The magnetic fields are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction
The net magnetic field is zero
The magnetic fields are equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Both the first and second options
explanation: At a neutral point the field of the magnet is exactly cancelled by the Earth's field (equal and opposite), so the net field there is zero — both statements describe it.

text: Electromagnets are:
options: Both permanent and made of steel
explanation: An electromagnet has a soft-iron core and is magnetised only while current flows, so it is a temporary magnet.

text: A current of 6.5 A flows through a conductor for 5 s. The charge passing through it is:
The material used for making the armature of an electric bell is:
explanation: Soft iron is magnetised and demagnetised easily, so the armature is attracted when current flows and released when it stops, letting the bell ring repeatedly.

text: Assertion (A): The resistance of a metallic conductor is constant at a given temperature. Reason (R): Metallic conductors obey Ohm's law.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Metallic conductors obey Ohm's law (V/I constant at constant temperature), which is exactly why their resistance is constant at a given temperature.

text: Which of the following is true for secondary cells?
options: Daniell cell and Leclanché cell are examples
They give current as a result of an irreversible chemical reaction
The only energy conversion is chemical to electrical
explanation: Secondary cells (e.g. lead-acid accumulator) have reversible reactions and can be recharged; Daniell and Leclanché cells are primary cells.

text: In a bar magnet, the magnetic field strength is minimum at the:
explanation: Magnetism is concentrated at the poles; the middle region of a bar magnet has the weakest field.

text: Which of the following is NOT true about an electromagnet?
options: It can be switched on and off
explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet — it loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

text: Assertion (A): A magnet attracts magnetic materials. Reason (R): Induction precedes attraction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true and R is false
A is false and R is true
explanation: A magnet first induces opposite polarity in the nearer end of a magnetic material, and then attracts it — so induction precedes, and explains, attraction.

text: An ammeter is used to:
explanation: An ammeter is connected in series to measure the current flowing in the circuit.

text: The resistance of a bulb filament with a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2 A through it is:

Identify the correct statement(s). Statement 1: A primary cell can give low as well as high current, whereas a secondary cell gives only a weak current. Statement 2: The internal resistance of primary cells is low and that of secondary cells is high.
explanation: Both are reversed: primary cells have high internal resistance and give only weak currents, while secondary cells have low internal resistance and can supply large currents.

text: Among the following, the incorrect statement(s) is/are: Statement 1: Magnetic field lines are open and continuous curves. Statement 2: Outside the magnet, magnetic field lines are directed from the south pole to the north pole.
explanation: Field lines are closed (not open) continuous curves, and outside a magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole. Both statements are incorrect.

text: If n electrons, each of charge e, pass through a cross-section of a conductor in time t, the current I is:
explanation: Total charge Q = ne, and current I = Q/t = ne/t.

text: The direction of the magnetic field at a point on a magnetic field line is given by the:
options: Line joining the point to the north pole
Normal to the line at that point
Line joining the point to the south pole
Tangent to the line at that point
explanation: The tangent drawn at any point on a field line gives the direction of the magnetic field at that point.

text: Electromagnets are made of:
explanation: Soft iron is used as the core because it is strongly magnetised while current flows and loses its magnetism quickly when the current stops.

text: Can two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
options: Yes, but only outside the magnet
No — at the point of intersection the field would have two directions, which is impossible
explanation: The magnetic field at a point has a unique direction (a compass points only one way), so two field lines can never cross.

text: Several soft iron pins can cling one below the other from the pole of a magnet. This is because:
options: Each pin becomes an induced magnet and in turn attracts the pin below it
explanation: By magnetic induction, the first pin becomes a magnet, which induces magnetism in the next pin, and so on, forming a chain.

text: The function of an ammeter in an electric circuit is to:
options: Measure the current flowing in the circuit
explanation: An ammeter, connected in series, measures the current through the circuit.

text: If 0.6 A flows through a resistor and the voltage across it is 12 V, its resistance is:
The SI units of potential difference (voltage) and electric current are respectively:
explanation: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (potential difference); 1 ampere = 1 coulomb of charge flowing per second (current).

text: An evidence of the existence of the Earth's magnetic field is that:
options: A freely suspended magnet (compass needle) always comes to rest pointing in the north-south direction
explanation: A freely suspended magnet aligns itself north-south, which shows that the Earth behaves like a huge magnet with its own magnetic field.

text: A compass needle placed at a neutral point:
explanation: At a neutral point the net magnetic field is zero, so there is no force aligning the needle and it can rest in any direction.

text: If 5 A of current flows through a conductor for 4 s, the charge passing through it is:
A charge of 20 C is transferred across a potential difference of 3 V. The work done is:
According to Ohm's law, the resistance R of a conductor is given by:
