explanation: Ohm's law states V ∝ I at constant temperature, i.e. V = IR, so R = V/I.

text: The physical quantity expressed in volts is:
explanation: The volt is the SI unit of potential difference (and of e.m.f.).

text: The SI unit of electrical resistance, 1 ohm, is the resistance of a conductor through which:
options: A charge of 1 C flows in 1 s
A current of 1 A flows for 1 s
A current of 1 A flows when a potential difference of 1 V is applied across it
1 J of work is done per coulomb
explanation: From R = V/I, 1 Ω = 1 V/1 A: a conductor has 1 ohm resistance if 1 V across it drives 1 A through it.

text: The SI unit of current and the direction of conventional current are:
options: Coulomb; the direction of electron flow
Ampere; the direction of flow of positive charge (opposite to electron flow)
Volt; from negative to positive terminal
Ampere; the direction of electron flow
explanation: Current is measured in amperes; conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal outside the cell, opposite to the flow of electrons.

text: A cell connected to a bulb has a potential difference of 24 V across it, and the ammeter reads 6 A. The resistance of the filament is:
The statement 'induced magnetism is temporary' means that:
options: The magnetism induced in a magnetic material disappears once the inducing magnet is removed
Induced magnetism cannot be produced in iron
explanation: A soft iron piece magnetised by induction loses (almost all) its magnetism when the magnet is taken away.

text: A solenoid with an iron core is connected to a battery and the core is strongly attracted into it. If the battery terminals are reversed, the iron core will:
options: Be repelled out of the solenoid
Still be attracted into the solenoid (only the polarity reverses)
Not be affected at all by the solenoid
explanation: Reversing the current reverses the solenoid's poles, but the soft iron core is induced with the matching opposite polarity, so it is still attracted.

text: If the number of turns in a solenoid's coil is increased (same current), the strength of the magnetic field it produces:
explanation: The magnetic field of a solenoid increases with the number of turns per unit length.

text: One difference between an electromagnet and a bar magnet is that:
options: A bar magnet is always stronger
An electromagnet is temporary and its strength can be varied, while a bar magnet is permanent with fixed strength
A bar magnet can be switched on and off
explanation: An electromagnet works only while current flows and its strength/polarity can be changed; a bar magnet's magnetism is permanent and fixed.

text: The function of a switch (key) in an electric circuit is to:
options: Open or close (break or complete) the circuit
explanation: A switch makes or breaks the circuit, starting or stopping the flow of current.

text: For a metallic conductor, an increase in (1) its length and (2) its temperature will:
options: Increase its resistance in both cases
Decrease its resistance in both cases
Increase it in case 1 and decrease it in case 2
explanation: R ∝ length, and for metals resistance increases with temperature, so both changes increase resistance.

text: One advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet is that:
options: Its strength can be controlled and it can be switched on and off
explanation: Varying the current changes an electromagnet's strength, and switching off the current removes its magnetism.

text: Which of the following is a use of an electromagnet in daily life?
options: In an electric bell and in cranes lifting scrap iron
explanation: Electromagnets are used in electric bells, cranes for scrap iron, electric motors, relays and loudspeakers.

text: Parallel and equidistant magnetic field lines represent a:
explanation: Field lines that are parallel and equally spaced show a field of the same strength and direction everywhere — a uniform field (e.g. the Earth's local field).

text: When the starter motor of a car is switched on for 0.8 s, a charge of 24 C passes through its coil. The current in the coil is:
Sam has a thick copper wire and Sonu a thin copper wire of the same length. Which wire has more resistance?
options: The thin wire (Sonu's), since resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area
explanation: R ∝ 1/A for the same material and length, so the thinner wire (smaller area) has greater resistance.

text: When current is drawn from a cell, the energy transformation taking place is:
explanation: Chemical reactions inside the cell release energy that drives charge round the circuit as electrical energy.

text: The unit joule per coulomb represents:
explanation: Potential difference = work done/charge, so J/C = volt.

text: If the resistance of a conductor is doubled while the potential difference across it is kept the same, the current:
explanation: I = V/R; with V fixed, doubling R halves I.

text: 'The potential difference between two conductors is 1 volt' means that:
options: 1 ampere flows through 1 ohm for 1 second
1 coulomb of charge flows per second
1 joule of work is done in moving 1 coulomb of charge from one conductor to the other
explanation: V = W/Q, so 1 V = 1 J/C: one joule of work is needed to move one coulomb of charge between the two points.

text: Two copper wires of the same cross-sectional area have lengths 3 cm and 9 cm. The ratio of their resistances is:
explanation: For the same material and area, R ∝ length, so R₁ : R₂ = 3 : 9 = 1 : 3.

text: A wire of resistance 12.5 Ω is connected to a battery of potential difference 2.5 V. The current in the circuit is:
An example of a secondary cell is the:
explanation: The lead-acid accumulator can be recharged, so it is a secondary cell; Leclanché, Daniell and dry cells are primary cells.

text: One difference between a concave mirror and a convex mirror is that:
options: A concave mirror converges light and can form real images, while a convex mirror diverges light and always forms virtual images
explanation: A concave (converging) mirror forms real or virtual images depending on object position; a convex (diverging) mirror always forms virtual, erect, diminished images.

text: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image distance is:
options: 6 cm in front of the mirror
explanation: With u = −15 cm and f = +10 cm: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/(−15) = 1/10 + 1/15 = 5/30 = 1/6, so v = +6 cm (behind the mirror, virtual).

text: The phenomenon by which a magnet makes nearby iron pieces magnets (e.g. iron nails forming a chain or being attracted as shown) is called:
explanation: Magnetic induction is the temporary magnetisation of a magnetic material in the presence of a magnet.
